Content:
In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of rounding to situations where we must round up instead of down.

Content:
For example, let's round [MATH: 127] to the nearest ten:

Content:
We begin by drawing a number line and plotting our number.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5a2526b5c4256e45ee3629ffff69c3c6]

Content:
Rounding a number to the nearest ten means finding the closest multiple of ten to our number.

Content:
The closest multiples of ten to [MATH: 127] are [MATH: 120] and [MATH: 130.] Let's add these multiples of [MATH: 10] to our diagram:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc2c147eb8c5e81415ee27c605a4db64]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: 127] is closer to [MATH: {\color{DarkGreen}130}] than [MATH: {\color{SaddleBrown}120},] this is the number we round to.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/187d3688433af432dedf4916933932d0]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 127] rounded to the nearest ten is [MATH: 130.]

Content:
We can also round whole numbers using place value charts.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's again round the following number to the nearest ten:

Content:
[MATH: 127]

Content:
We start by writing our number's digits in a place value chart. Since we're rounding to the nearest ten, we highlight the tens place:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 7] |

Content:
We then look one digit to the right in the chart (this will be the ones place) and compare it to the number [MATH: 5{:}]

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}7}] |

Content:
Now, since [MATH: \color{red}7] is greater or equal to [MATH: 5], we must round up. To do this, we follow two steps:

Content:
- We put [MATH: \color{blue}0] into the ones place:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] |

Content:
- Then, we increase the tens value by one:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3}] | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 127] rounded to the nearest ten is [MATH: 130.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Rounding a number to the nearest ten means finding the closest multiple of ten to our number.

Content:
The closest multiples of ten to [MATH: 127] are [MATH: 120] and [MATH: 130.] Let's add these multiples of [MATH: 10] to our diagram:

[IMG: /graphics/fc2c147eb8c5e81415ee27c605a4db64]

Item 2 — Tutorial: Recognizing Multiples of 10 and 100

- Multiples of [MATH: 10] always end in at least one zero.

[MATH: 20, \qquad 80, \qquad 110, \qquad 200]

Content:
- Multiples of [MATH: 100] always end in at least two zeros.

For example, all the following numbers are multiples of [MATH: 100{:}]
[MATH: 100, \qquad 500, \qquad 2,100, \qquad 3,000]
